query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a trace (≈0.1 wt %) of aligned graphene nanoplatelets at the W–Cu phase boundaries of a spark-plasma-sintered (SPS) W–Cu metal-matrix composite will raise the room-temperature bulk thermal conductivity by ≈20 % without reducing flexural strength (>90 % of baseline) or irradiation-induced swelling resistance after 1 dpa neutron or ion exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional W–40 vol % Cu composite fabricated by liquid-phase infiltration, density ≥98 % theoretical, grain size W ≈3 µm, Cu network continuous.
generation.intervention: Disperse 0.1 wt % graphene nanoplatelets, oriented parallel to the anticipated heat-flux direction, at W/Cu interfaces via ball milling followed by rapid densification with SPS (<10 min at 1000 °C, 50 MPa).
generation.conditions: Operating from 25 °C to 600 °C under steady heat fluxes up to 10 MW m⁻² and neutron or ion irradiation producing ≤1 dpa damage at ≤600 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Two-dimensional graphene layers forming continuous, high-conductivity bridges across W–Cu interfaces and acting as defect-sink sinks during irradiation.
generation.mechanism: 1) Graphene’s in-plane κ ≫ 1000 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ provides parallel heat-conduction channels, lowering Kapitza resistance at W/Cu interfaces. 2) The small addition (<0.5 vol %) minimally perturbs load-bearing W skeleton, preserving strength. 3) Graphene’s high vacancy binding and sink efficiency absorb point defects, mitigating irradiation swelling.
generation.predicted_outcome: Composite κ increases from ~220 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (baseline) to ≥260 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ at 25 °C and maintains ≥200 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ after 1 dpa. Room-temperature four-point-bending strength remains ≥450 MPa (≥90 % of baseline). Swelling and hardness change after irradiation remain within ±10 % of baseline.
generation.baseline: Identical W–40 vol % Cu composite processed by SPS under the same conditions but without graphene addition.
generation.boundary: Benefits expected only when graphene content is 0.05–0.3 wt %, nanoplatelets are ≥1 µm lateral size with aspect ratio >100, and processing temperature ≤1100 °C (to avoid carbon dissolution). Above 800 °C service temperature or >3 dpa damage, graphene degradation may negate gains.
generation.uncertainty: No direct prior study on graphene-modified W–Cu; magnitude of κ gain and irradiation tolerance extrapolated from Cu–graphene and W–graphite interface data, so predicted values may deviate by ±50 %.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two SPS compacts: (A) baseline W–40 vol % Cu; (B) identical but with 0.1 wt % aligned graphene. Measure (i) room-temperature κ by laser flash, (ii) four-point-bending strength, (iii) κ and swelling after 1 dpa 2 MeV Cu-ion irradiation at 600 °C.
measurements: Room-temperature thermal diffusivity and calculated κ
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Hypothesis is falsified if sample B shows (i) ≤5 % higher κ than A before irradiation OR (ii) bending strength <90 % of A OR (iii) post-irradiation κ drop >25 % relative to pre-irradiation value.
